question: Which South Carolina agency handles vessel registration and titling for motorboats operated on the state's public waters?
choice_a: The South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SCDNR)
choice_b: The South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles
choice_c: The U.S. Coast Guard exclusively, with no state role at all
choice_d: County sheriff's offices individually issue all vessel titles
explanation: SCDNR handles vessel registration and titling in South Carolina, issuing the registration numbers and decals that must be properly displayed on a motorboat operated on the state's public waters, under the framework of S.C. Code Title 50, Chapter 21.
source_note: SCDNR vessel registration and titling program (dnr.sc.gov), S.C. Code Ann. Title 50, Chapter 21

question: Where must a South Carolina vessel's registration number be displayed on the hull?
choice_a: South Carolina vessels are not required to display a registration number
choice_b: On each side of the forward half of the vessel, in plain, block characters that contrast with the hull color and are legible from a reasonable distance
choice_c: Anywhere on the vessel, including the underside of the hull where it cannot be seen while afloat
choice_d: Only on paperwork kept inside a dry bag, never on the hull itself
explanation: South Carolina, like other states following the federal numbering system standard, requires the registration number to be painted or permanently attached to each side of the forward half of the vessel in plain, legible block characters that contrast with the hull's background color.
source_note: Federal vessel numbering display standards (33 CFR 174) applied under South Carolina's registration/titling framework

question: What must a South Carolina boater carry aboard the vessel to prove current, valid registration while on the water?
choice_a: Only a receipt from the vessel's original purchase, regardless of age
choice_b: A copy of the operator's boater education certificate satisfies the registration requirement
choice_c: The current certificate of registration (or a copy), available for inspection by an SCDNR officer or other authorized law enforcement
choice_d: Nothing; registration never needs to be proven on the water
explanation: A South Carolina boater should have the vessel's current certificate of registration (or a valid copy) aboard and available to show an SCDNR officer or other law enforcement upon request during a routine safety check or inspection.

question: Under South Carolina's PWC rules (Section 50-21-870), when is PWC operation prohibited regardless of the operator's certification?
choice_a: PWCs may legally operate at any hour of the day or night with no restriction
explanation: Section 50-21-870 prohibits PWC operation from sunset to sunrise regardless of the operator's certification status, reflecting the added risk of operating a small, low-visibility, high-maneuverability craft after dark.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-870 (PWC sunset-to-sunrise prohibition)

question: Under Section 50-21-870, what restriction applies to "wake surfing" or similar close-following activity near moored vessels or docks?
choice_a: It is restricted to idle speed within 200 feet of moored vessels or docks
choice_b: Wake surfing is entirely unregulated near docks and moored vessels
choice_c: It is only restricted at night
choice_d: It is banned everywhere in South Carolina at all times
explanation: Section 50-21-870 restricts activities like wake surfing to idle speed within 200 feet of moored vessels or docks, reducing the risk that a large following wake will rock or damage nearby boats and structures.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-870 (wake surfing / close-proximity speed restriction)

question: What does South Carolina's PWC statute say about chasing or harassing wildlife while operating a personal watercraft?
choice_a: The statute is silent on the subject entirely
choice_c: It is explicitly permitted and encouraged as a recreational activity
choice_d: It is only prohibited if the wildlife is a protected species
explanation: Section 50-21-870 prohibits using a PWC to chase or harass wildlife, both to protect animals from stress and injury and to prevent the unsafe, unpredictable maneuvering such chasing tends to involve.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-870 (wildlife harassment prohibition)

question: What must every occupant of a South Carolina PWC do at all times under Section 50-21-870, regardless of swimming ability?
choice_a: Wear a full wetsuit but no PFD
choice_b: Only wear a PFD if operating more than one mile from shore
choice_c: Wear a properly fastened, Coast Guard-approved personal flotation device
choice_d: Nothing; PFDs are optional for experienced swimmers on a PWC
explanation: Section 50-21-870 requires every PWC occupant, operator and passengers alike, to wear a Coast Guard-approved PFD at all times while underway, without exception for swimming ability or distance from shore.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-870 (PWC PFD requirement)

question: How often must a South Carolina vessel registration typically be renewed to remain current?
choice_a: Vessel registration in South Carolina never expires once issued
choice_b: Registration must be renewed every single day
choice_c: Renewal is entirely optional with no legal consequence for lapsing
choice_d: On a periodic renewal cycle set by SCDNR, requiring the owner to renew before the registration's expiration date to avoid operating with a lapsed registration
explanation: Like most states, South Carolina vessel registrations run on a periodic renewal cycle administered by SCDNR; an owner who fails to renew before expiration risks operating with a lapsed registration, which can result in a citation, so boaters should confirm the current renewal period and fee schedule directly with SCDNR.
source_note: SCDNR vessel registration renewal program (dnr.sc.gov), general renewal-cycle framework

question: Why does South Carolina require an engine cutoff lanyard to be attached to a PWC operator under Section 50-21-870, beyond simply requiring a PFD?
choice_a: If the operator is thrown from the PWC, the lanyard automatically shuts off the engine, preventing a riderless PWC from circling back and striking the person in the water
choice_b: The lanyard exists purely as a decorative safety feature with no functional purpose
choice_c: The lanyard is required only to prevent theft of the PWC
choice_d: The lanyard replaces the need for a PFD entirely
explanation: A PWC's engine cutoff lanyard is a critical safety feature distinct from PFD requirements: if the operator falls off, the lanyard detaches and kills the engine, preventing the classic and dangerous scenario of a riderless PWC circling back at speed toward the person who fell off.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-870 (engine cutoff lanyard requirement) and universal PWC safety rationale

question: Does a PWC operator in South Carolina need to comply with the state's general boater education mandate under Section 50-21-95?
choice_a: The education mandate applies only to sailboats
choice_b: Yes -- PWCs are explicitly named alongside motorboats of 10 hp or more and specialty propcraft as vessel types covered by the education requirement for operators born on or after July 1, 2007
choice_c: No, PWCs are entirely exempt from the boater education mandate
choice_d: Only PWC passengers, never the operator, must complete the course
explanation: South Carolina's boater education mandate explicitly names PWCs alongside sufficiently powered motorboats and specialty propcraft as vessel types requiring an approved boater education certificate for operators born on or after July 1, 2007.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-95 (PWC inclusion in the boater education mandate)

question: What is a practical reason a South Carolina boat owner should keep their SCDNR registration decal and hull number legible and up to date?
choice_a: A faded decal automatically extends the registration period
choice_b: Only decals on trailers, never on the boat itself, are ever checked
choice_c: It helps identify the vessel to enforcement, rescue, and registration authorities, and an illegible or expired decal can result in a citation during a routine safety check
choice_d: Registration decals serve no practical or legal purpose once initially applied
explanation: A legible, current registration decal and properly displayed hull number let SCDNR officers, other law enforcement, and rescue personnel quickly identify a vessel and confirm it is properly registered; an illegible or expired decal is a common and easily avoidable basis for a citation.
source_note: SCDNR vessel registration and enforcement guidance (dnr.sc.gov)
